bib.title: Chapter 1. Agentic AI and MCP (AI Agents with MCP, O'Reilly Early Release)

question: What is an agent, how do agents differ from workflows, and where does MCP fit in agentic AI?
contributions: Explains MCP as an M+N fix for the MxN connector problem
Names other agent protocols (A2A, ACP, ANP)

results.claim: Without a common protocol, M models and N tools need M x N connectors; the chapter's example is 3 models and 4 tools needing 12.
results.setup: 3 models, 4 tools, one connector per pair, no MCP
results.quote: If you support 3 models and 4 tools, that means you have to write 12 connectors

results.claim: With MCP the same 3 models and 4 tools need 7 connectors (M + N).
results.setup: 3 models, 4 tools, each model has a client and each tool an MCP server
results.quote: we only need 7 connectors instead of 12

limits: Early Release draft, raw and unedited; no experiments or data.
Author names are not printed in the PDF text.
Protocol landscape claims (A2A, ACP, ANP) are brief and dated to mid-2025.
practices: Define an agent as an LLM that dynamically directs its own process and tool use, following Anthropic's Building Effective Agents (Agent section).
Use a workflow, where code decides the path, when a task needs deterministic logic; use an agent when the LLM should choose tools over one or more action-feedback loops (Agent section).
Expose tools through MCP servers so any tool-capable model connects via one client rather than per-model connectors (MCP's Role section).
Treat MCP and A2A as complements: MCP for tools and data, A2A for agent-to-agent communication (Other Protocols section).

terms.definition: system where large language models dynamically direct their own processes and tool usage, maintaining control over how they accomplish tasks
any code outside of the agent that is called by the agent to accomplish some task
the LLM does some action, feedback is gathered and sent back, and the LLM decides to present a final result, act again, or ask the user
a system in which code, rather than the LLM, determines the path the logic will take, but still calls an LLM for part of the work
workflow pattern for tasks needing one or more LLM calls and a code path deciding next steps
several LLM calls are made at once and results combined
an LLM classifies an input then makes one of several possible LLM calls
one LLM breaks down a task, calls worker LLMs, and an LLM puts results together
an LLM generates a response and a second call evaluates it, accepting or returning it with feedback
for each of M LLMs supported, N connectors are needed for each tool or data source
server provides tools, prompts, data resources; client connects a host application to a server; transport is the communication protocol between them
endpoints every tool-supporting server exposes; the host calls them via its client to list and call tools
